cards.title: Judging names is the scarce skill, not generating them
cards.summary: AI can mass-produce name candidates, so the durable advantage shifts to your ability to judge which names are right versus merely okay.
cards.use_when: When naming a new product, brand line, or store, or when you have a longlist of candidates and need to pick the one to launch with.
steps: Generate a wide longlist of candidate names with AI or a group brainstorm; the naming expert behind BlackBerry, Febreze and Swiffer notes that anyone can now generate 200-300 names with AI tools, so generation is no longer the bottleneck.

Instead of spending your time generating more, invest it in building a judgment framework: define what 'right' means for this product before you evaluate, so the criteria are not reverse-engineered from whichever names you happen to like.
Score each candidate against that framework rather than arguing pairwise. The source's point is that separating the right names from the good and the okay names is where the value now sits.
Apply the same judgment to each candidate: does it fit the product category, the positioning line you intend, and the customer's vocabulary?
Keep the rejected-but-good names in a file; they may suit a future SKU or sub-brand.
caveats: The source runs a naming firm whose competitive advantage is proprietary data and software integrated with AI; a small brand will not replicate that dataset, so allocate more weight to your own category and customer knowledge.

cards.title: Budget and scope for professional naming work
cards.summary: Name-development projects from an established naming firm typically run roughly $75k to $150k, with large corporate programs reaching about $200k, and usually include more than just the name.
cards.use_when: When planning budget, scope, or an in-house vs agency decision for a new brand, product line, or flagship SKU.
steps: Treat these numbers as a directional benchmark from one firm, not a market rate. The source describes most projects landing between a low of about $75k and a high of about $150k, with big corporate work up to roughly $200k.
Expect the deliverable to extend beyond the name: the source describes helping with nomenclature (how the product is defined), a positioning line, and a short brand story.
Ask about tracking research: the firm runs small quantitative studies monitoring how the name lands over roughly 90-120 days after launch.
If your budget cannot support this tier, decide explicitly which parts you can do yourself (name generation, positioning line) and where you will buy expertise (qualitative validation, tracking).
Convert the fee into a per-year cost if the name will be used for years, and compare it against the cost of a later rename: packaging, listings, domain, ad creative, and accumulated search equity.
caveats: These are one firm's 2026-era numbers for consulting projects; costs vary widely by region, scope and firm size.
Small ecommerce brands rarely need this spend for every SKU; reserve it for the flagship or umbrella brand.

cards.title: Name launches usually include a post-launch tracking study
cards.summary: After delivering a name, naming firms often run small quantitative tracking research over 90-120 days to see how the name is landing with the market.
cards.use_when: When you have just launched or rebranded and want to know whether the new name is gaining traction before locking in packaging, listings and ad spend.
steps: Define a small set of measurable signals before launch: unaided and aided recall of the name, correct association with the product category, and how easily it is repeated or spelled when someone hears it.
Run a lightweight survey at launch and again at roughly 90-120 days; the source describes exactly this cadence as typical tracking research.
Include a practical commerce signal: can people find the store by searching the name, and does the paid-search auction for the name show rising volume?
Watch for name-specific failure modes: misspellings in search queries, voice-assistant mishearing, and people confusing the name with an existing brand.
Decide in advance what result triggers action: if recall and category association do not improve materially by the second wave, weigh the cost of a repositioning line versus a full rename.
Feed findings back into the positioning line and short brand story rather than changing the name reflexively.
caveats: The source describes the practice but gives no numeric thresholds; choose your own meaningful improvement level.
Small samples can be noisy, so treat the second wave as directional.

cards.title: Use 'approximate thinking' to unlock team creativity
cards.summary: Draw a line with bizarre/absurd/illegal ideas on one end and safe workable ideas on the other, put 'approximate thinking' in the middle, and explicitly give people permission to stop there instead of jumping straight to safe answers.
cards.use_when: When briefing your team or an agency on ad creative, product naming, landing-page concepts, or any ideation session where output has become predictable.
steps: Draw the spectrum: on one end bizarre, absurd or even illegal ideas; on the other, safe workable ideas. Write 'approximate thinking' in the middle and show it to your team.
Explain the rule: you may move from bizarre through approximate, then stop there. Do not force the jump to finished, safe ideas.
Present the approximate set deliberately unfinished: not baked out, not full, possibly bad. The source states that giving people permission to work at this stage makes creativity spike.
As the operator, resist killing an idea because it is not yet a campaign. Ask instead: what would have to be true for this to work?
Select a small number of approximate ideas to develop further into ads, PDP copy, or bundles, and keep the bizarre end visible so the safe end does not become the whole range.
Repeat the exercise each time the output gets stale rather than only once.
caveats: This is the source's own coaching device for creative teams, not a documented experiment; expect to sift a lot of unusable material.
Not every category can absorb a bizarre concept, and in regulated categories legal review still applies.

cards.title: Give AI the generation work, keep the judgment in-house
cards.summary: Integrating AI into a naming process took one firm about 16 months and shifted its edge from producing names to judging them against proprietary data.
cards.use_when: When deciding how far to automate naming, product-copy generation, or creative concepts, and what capability to keep human.
steps: Use AI to widen the funnel cheaply: the source notes anyone can now generate 200-300 names with assistants such as ChatGPT or Claude. Treat that output as raw material, not decisions.
Build the judgment layer yourself: define the criteria, the category conventions, and the customer vocabulary that a name or concept must satisfy.

Invest in the data that makes judgment repeatable: the source firm spent about 16 months integrating AI into a database it had already invested in. For a retailer, that may be search-query logs, review language and returns reasons rather than a naming database.
Note the source's observation that six of roughly twelve or thirteen active projects were AI-driven, i.e. even an established naming practice is restructuring around the technology.
Assign a single owner to final judgment so AI output does not get adopted by whoever generated the most options.
caveats: The 16-month integration and the project mix are one firm's experience, not a productivity benchmark.
AI output may reproduce existing or trademarked names; run clearance checks before committing to anything.
